lesson.subtitle: Lesson 21 -- Conditional Structures in Negotiations
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Eduarda | Lesson 21 -- Conditional Structures in Negotiations

listenings.text: Hi Eduarda, it's James. A few thoughts before your call with Northgate tomorrow. Don't accept their first number. Eighty million is only an anchor. Remember our leverage: we have a second buyer. If they offered ninety million upfront, I would take it to the client. If they stayed at eighty, I would walk away, but only after you test the earn-out. Make it clear that any earn-out is contingent on keeping the management team. And speak in hypotheticals: if you paid this, we would do that. It gives you room to move without making a firm promise. Call me after the meeting.

Here is a simple rule for any negotiation. Never give something without getting something back. That is a trade-off, and the grammar helps you make it. Use the second conditional to test an idea: if you extended the deadline, we would lower the price. It sounds like a question, not a commitment. When you are ready to commit, switch to the first conditional: if you sign this week, we will include the warranty. And when you need a firm condition, use provided that or as long as: we will agree, provided that the payment is made in cash. Finally, always know your fallback option before you sit down. Without it, you have no leverage.

extra_audio.text: Eduarda refused to accept the buyer's anchor of eighty million. She reminded Daniel that her client had a fallback option. She tested an idea: if part of the price were an earn-out, both sides would win. Daniel agreed, provided that the targets were realistic. They made the deal contingent on keeping the management team. Finally, they met halfway at ninety million upfront.
